title: Oromo Muqmad (Dried Beef)
community: Oromo pastoralists — the preserved meat tradition
author: Mama Tigist

meta.cookingMethod: Slow Cooked and Preserved in Fat

desc: Oromo Muqmad — beef cut into strips, slow-cooked with berbere and spices, then preserved in melted kibbeh fat in clay pots. The Oromo confit — the traditional preserved meat that pastoralist communities prepare for long journeys and lean seasons.
longDesc: Muqmad is the Oromo answer to food preservation — beef cooked in its own fat and spices until completely tender, then submerged in kibbeh to create an airtight seal. Kept in clay pots, it lasts months without refrigeration.
ingredients: // Preservation: additional 3—4 tbsp kibbeh for sealing
equipment: Clay pot or jar for storage
steps: Toss beef strips with berbere, salt, and mitmita.
Place in a heavy pot. Cook over medium-low heat in their own fat and kibbeh 45—60 minutes.
Beef should be completely tender and fat-rendered.
Transfer to a clean clay pot or jar.
Pour hot kibbeh over to completely submerge the beef.
Seal with a cloth. Cool. Store in a cool, dark place.
chefTips: Complete submersion in fat is the preservation technique.
The kibbeh seal must have no air pockets.
cookingScience: Muqmad is a confit preparation — immersion in fat (kibbeh) removes oxygen, which is required for most bacterial and fungal growth. The high salt and berbere content further inhibit microbial activity. This is one of the world's oldest and most effective meat preservation methods.
sustainabilityTips: Traditional preservation without refrigeration — zero energy use.
storage: In fat-sealed clay pot: months without refrigeration.
reheating: Remove from fat. Cook in a pan.
culturalNote: Muqmad is the food of the Oromo pastoralist's long journey — prepared before cattle drives, before long seasonal migrations, and before any period of uncertain food supply. It represents the Oromo people's mastery of their environment.
